paragraphs.text: Spastic paraplegia-51 is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder belonging to the AP-4 deficiency syndrome. It is characterized by severe intellectual disability with absent or very limited speech, microcephaly, and infantile hypotonia that progresses to spastic paraplegia or tetraplegia, so that patients do not walk or become wheelchair-bound. Other features include stereotypic laughter, drooling, short stature, and, in some patients, seizures (Moreno-De-Luca et al., 2011; Abou Jamra et al., 2011; Kong et al., 2013).

checks.explanation: The paper calls the disorder autosomal recessive; cerebral palsy is described as a neurodevelopmental disorder.

checks.claim: Spastic paraplegia-51 belongs to the AP-4 deficiency syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) reported 2 sibs, a woman and a man, from a consanguineous Palestinian-Jordanian family. The sister (IV-4) was born after a full-term pregnancy with an uneventful labor and delivery. At birth she had microcephaly and hypotonia, which progressed to spastic tetraplegia with hyperreflexia and generalized hypertonia by the first year of life. She never developed speech, had been wheelchair-bound since age 5 years, and had generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Examination at age 23 showed microcephaly (-3 SD), profound cognitive impairment, adaptive skills with age equivalents below 1 year, drooling, outbursts of stereotypic laughter, absent sphincter control, and a Babinski sign. Her dysmorphic features included bitemporal narrowing, a long narrow face, a prominent pointed chin, downslanting palpebral fissures, a long nose with a wide nasal ridge, a short philtrum, an everted full upper vermilion, a prominent antihelix, and facial hypotonia. Brain imaging showed ventriculomegaly, cortical and cerebellar atrophy, reduced hippocampal volume, and diffuse white matter loss that was more pronounced frontally and in the corpus callosum. EEG showed generalized theta slowing. Eye evaluation and hearing were normal.

paragraphs.text: Her brother (IV-5) had microcephaly and hypotonia postnatally, and developmental delay was evident by the first year of life. He acquired some dysarthric words but never normal speech. He was able to walk with support, but increasing spasticity made him wheelchair-dependent by age 9 years. His seizures began as staring spells and became generalized tonic-clonic at age 15. On examination at 22 years he had microcephaly (-3 SD), severe cognitive deficits, spastic tetraplegia with hypertonia, hyperreflexia and a Babinski sign, outbursts of stereotypic laughter, drooling, jerky nystagmus, and absent sphincter control. A head CT scan showed moderate ventriculomegaly with slightly prominent cisterns. Eye evaluation and hearing were normal (Moreno-De-Luca et al., 2011).

paragraphs.text: Abou Jamra et al. (2011) reported 8 affected individuals from 3 consanguineous families. Each family had a mutation in a different AP4 subunit gene, one of which was AP4E1. The patients had severe intellectual disability, absent speech, a shy character, stereotypic laughter, muscular hypotonia that progressed to spastic paraplegia, microcephaly, foot deformity, decreased muscle mass of the lower limbs, inability to walk, and growth retardation. The abstract did not separate the features of the AP4E1 family from those of the other 2 families. The authors concluded that AP4 deficiency causes a clinically recognizable syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) reported identical twin girls (P1 and P2) born to first-cousin Moroccan parents. Both had neonatal asphyxia and early infantile hypotonia. When examined at age 3 years, they had marked developmental retardation and microcephaly (head circumference 46 cm (-2 SD) in P1 and 45.5 cm (-2.5 SD) in P2). Other findings were intellectual disability, spastic paraplegia of the lower limbs, inability to walk unaided, and failure to acquire normal speech. They also had short stature, low body weight, drooling, stereotypic laughter, pseudobulbar signs (jaw jerk and gag reflex), absent sphincter control, and loss of acquired function. Their facial features were coarse, with a prominent bulbous nose and a wide mouth. Brain imaging showed cortical atrophy and atrophy of the inferior vermis, and EEG showed diffuse slow waves. Neither twin had seizures, involuntary movements, contractures, hyperreflexia, a Babinski sign, or hypertonia. P1 had slight myopia, astigmatism, and conductive hearing loss on the left side. P2 had slight astigmatism.

(2011) used chromosomal microarray analysis to identify a homozygous deletion at chromosome 15q21.2 (see). The deletion was 139 kb at minimum and 222 kb at maximum, and fine-mapping defined it as 192 kb (chr15:48835480-49028171, hg18). paragraphs.text: In identical twin girls born to first-cousin Moroccan parents, Kong et al. (2013) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous nonsense mutation in the AP4E1 gene (R1105X). The twins had complex hereditary spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability, microcephaly, and short stature. The mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The parents were heterozygous, a healthy sib was wild-type, and the variant was absent from 1,050 CEPH controls and 69 Moroccan controls. In patient EBV-B cells, the mutation did not affect AP4E1 mRNA levels or splicing. However, AP-4-epsilon protein was barely detectable, and AP-4-beta and AP-4-mu levels were also decreased. Native immunoprecipitation showed a more than 95% reduction in assembled AP-4 complex in patient fibroblasts and EBV-B cells. The AP-4-binding partner tepsin was undetectable in patient fibroblasts. One twin was also heterozygous for missense variants in IFNGR1 (Q190R) and IL12RB2 (K768N), which the authors did not consider causal.

On this basis they proposed that disruption of any of the 4 subunits causes a distinct autosomal recessive AP-4 deficiency syndrome. Abou Jamra et al. (2011) noted that adaptor protein complexes AP1 to AP4 are ubiquitously expressed, evolutionarily conserved heterotetrameric complexes. These complexes mediate different types of vesicle formation and select the cargo molecules included in the vesicles. Abou Jamra et al. (2011) suggested that AP4-mediated trafficking plays a crucial role in brain development and function.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) studied identical twin girls born to first-cousin Moroccan parents. The twins had complex hereditary spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability, microcephaly, and short stature, as well as BCG lymphadenitis. Using whole-exome sequencing, the authors identified a homozygous arg1105-to-ter (R1105X) mutation in the AP4E1 gene in both twins, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The parents were heterozygous, and a healthy sib was wild-type. The mutation was not found in 1,050 CEPH controls or in 69 Moroccan controls. It did not affect AP4E1 mRNA levels or splicing in patient EBV-B cells, but AP-4-epsilon protein was barely detectable, and AP-4-beta and AP-4-mu levels were also decreased. Assembled AP-4 complex was reduced by more than 95% in patient fibroblasts and EBV-B cells, and tepsin was undetectable in patient fibroblasts.
